annotation_description: Choosing to be on the draw is almost always wrong in competitive Magic, especially with a hand full of discard spells (Thoughtseize, Inquisition of Kozilek). Being on the play lets you strip key cards from the opponent's hand before they can use them on turn 1, which is the entire point of running these spells. The reasoning given ('being on the draw gives us an extra card') is a common misconception — in Modern, tempo and the ability to interact before the opponent's first meaningful turn is far more valuable than the extra card, particularly with proactive disruption like hand attack.

Playing Swamp instead of Marsh Flats is slightly suboptimal. With Thoughtseize and Inquisition of Kozilek both in hand (wanting to cast a discard spell this turn), any of the black sources work. However, Marsh Flats is generally better to play first because: (1) it thins the deck, (2) it can fetch Swamp anyway, and (3) you have Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth which will make all lands Swamps later, making Marsh Flats unable to tap for colored mana without fetching. Additionally, against an artifact deck (Mox Opal, Mishra's Bauble suggest Emry/artifact strategies), cracking Marsh Flats now preserves the option to play Ifnir Deadlands or Urborg later when they're more relevant. The Swamp in hand becomes a worse draw-equivalent later compared to having already thinned with Marsh Flats.

Against an artifact-based deck (Mox Opal, Mishra's Bauble visible), Inquisition of Kozilek likely hits most relevant cards since artifact strategies tend to be low-curve. The opponent's deck appears to run cards like Emry (CMC 3), Welding Jar (CMC 0), Weapons Manufacturing (CMC 2), and other cheap artifacts - almost all hittable by Inquisition. Paying 2 life with Thoughtseize is unnecessary when Inquisition would likely see and hit the same targets. The 2 life matters against aggressive artifact strategies that can deal incidental damage.

The opponent's hand contains Emry, Lurker of the Loch, which is the engine that ties their entire artifact recursion strategy together. Emry with Mox Opal and Welding Jar gives them metalcraft immediately, and Emry can recur Mishra's Bauble from the graveyard repeatedly for card advantage. Weapons Manufacturing is strong but requires other artifacts to enter to generate value. Taking Emry shuts down their recursion engine and leaves them with enchantments that need artifacts to trigger, while the player has Inquisition of Kozilek in hand to potentially take another piece next turn.

The opponent cast Thoughtseize targeting Gem25F Libby, and Libby is being asked to select a target for Mishra's Bauble's activated ability (which is a separate item on the stack). However, looking more carefully at the decision, Libby is choosing who to target with Mishra's Bauble - themselves or the opponent. Targeting yourself with Mishra's Bauble when you could instead look at the top card of your opponent's library is a significant missed opportunity. Knowing what your opponent will draw next turn provides much more strategic value than knowing your own top card, especially early in the game when you have no scry or library manipulation to take advantage of that information. The reasoning given ('to better organize my own library') doesn't even make sense since Mishra's Bauble doesn't reorganize your library - it only lets you look at the top card.

Playing a second Mox Opal while the first is on the battlefield violates the Legend Rule - one must be sacrificed immediately. The player has only 1 artifact on the battlefield (the first Mox Opal), so even after the second enters and one is sacrificed, they'll still have just 1 artifact, far from the 3 needed for Metalcraft. This wastes a Mox Opal for no mana benefit. The correct sequence would be to play Welding Jar first (free artifact, getting to 2 artifacts), then play the land (Fiery Islet), then cast Emry (who costs {U} with 2 artifacts via Affinity), which mills 4 cards and adds another artifact creature. After Emry, Metalcraft would be active with 3+ artifacts, making the single Mox Opal functional.

Playing Fiery Islet before Welding Jar means Mox Opal doesn't have Metalcraft active this turn (only 1 artifact on battlefield). Playing Welding Jar first would give 2 artifacts, and then Engineered Explosives for 0 would give 3 artifacts, enabling Metalcraft on Mox Opal. With Metalcraft active, the player could potentially cast Emry (which has affinity for artifacts, costing less with 3+ artifacts) this turn. The sequencing of land before artifact here delays achieving Metalcraft and potentially delays the Emry play.

Playing Marsh Flats instead of Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth as the turn 2 land drop. Urborg would provide {B} for Inquisition of Kozilek without any life cost, while also making Ifnir Deadlands tap for {B} freely on future turns. Playing Marsh Flats means either cracking it (losing 1 life unnecessarily) or holding it uncracked, wasting a more valuable resource.

Casting Nethergoyf before Inquisition of Kozilek is suboptimal sequencing. Inquisition of Kozilek should be cast first because: (1) It reveals the opponent's hand, giving crucial information about what threats/answers they have (like Emry, Engineered Explosives, etc.), which could inform whether to deploy Nethergoyf now or hold it. (2) After Inquisition resolves, there will be a sorcery (Inquisition) in the graveyard alongside the existing sorcery (Thoughtseize), but more importantly the opponent's discarded card could matter for planning. (3) Nethergoyf currently has power equal to the number of card types in the graveyard - right now there's just Sorcery (Thoughtseize), so it's a 1/2. Casting Inquisition first doesn't change this since it's also a sorcery. However, the information from Inquisition could reveal whether it's even safe to deploy Nethergoyf (e.g., opponent might have Engineered Explosives which could answer it). Playing the discard spell first is a fundamental sequencing principle - gather information before committing threats.

Playing Claws of Gix before Emry is suboptimal sequencing. With Mox Opal, Welding Jar, and Claws of Gix, they have 3 artifacts for Metalcraft on Mox Opal, but Emry with Affinity for artifacts already costs only U with 3 artifacts (Mox Opal, Welding Jar, Claws of Gix). However, the better line is to cast Emry first: with 3 artifacts already (Mox Opal, Welding Jar, + Claws of Gix cast first), Emry costs U. But actually, without Claws of Gix, they have 2 artifacts (Mox Opal, Welding Jar), so Emry costs 1U. They can tap Fiery Islet for U and need 1 more generic - but Mox Opal doesn't have Metalcraft with only 2 artifacts. So casting Claws of Gix first enables Metalcraft on Mox Opal, then they can tap both Mox Opal and Fiery Islet to cast Emry for 1U (reduced to U by 3 artifacts = free with affinity... wait: Emry costs 2U, with 3 artifacts affinity reduces by 2, so it costs U). With Metalcraft active, Mox Opal taps for any color. So Claws first, then Emry for U off Fiery Islet works. But they could also cast Emry for U and then Claws of Gix after. Actually the key question is: they played Claws of Gix and then skipped their attack and apparently didn't cast Emry. With Claws on the field (3 artifacts), Mox Opal has Metalcraft, they can tap Fiery Islet for U to cast Emry (cost reduced from 2U to U). They should have followed up with Emry to mill four cards and start recurring artifacts. Not casting Emry this turn when they could is the real missed opportunity.

Nethergoyf was likely cast on a previous turn (turn 2) and would not have summoning sickness. It's a 2/3 attacking into an empty board for free damage. The player incorrectly assumed it had summoning sickness.

Playing Urza's Saga instead of Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth means only one disruption spell can be cast this turn instead of potentially two. With Urborg providing a third black source, both Thoughtseize and Inquisition of Kozilek could be cast this turn to strip the opponent's hand. Urza's Saga could be played next turn instead.

The player chose Thoughtseize over Inquisition of Kozilek when both were in hand. Looking at the opponent's board state, they have cheap artifacts and an Engineered Explosives. The opponent's likely threats include cards like Emry (CMC 3) and Kappa Cannoneer (CMC 6). Inquisition of Kozilek hits everything CMC 3 or less without the 2 life cost. Since the player is already at 17 life and has Thoughtseize available for later when they might need to hit a high-CMC card, using Inquisition first would save 2 life while likely hitting the same targets. The 2 life matters especially with Ifnir Deadlands also costing life. However, Thoughtseize does guarantee hitting Kappa Cannoneer if it's in hand, which Inquisition cannot. This is a reasonable consideration, but typically the correct sequencing is to use Inquisition first to save life and save Thoughtseize for when you specifically need to hit something above CMC 3.

Nethergoyf costs only {B} and Sonnet Coach has had Swamps available since early turns. By Turn 4, Nethergoyf almost certainly does not have summoning sickness. The player incorrectly assumed it did and missed attacking with a 2/3 into an empty board for 2 free damage.

The reasoning mentions destroying 'mana value 2' permanents, but Nethergoyf costs {B} (mana value 1). If Engineered Explosives had 2 charge counters (from spending U and R via Fiery Islet/Mox Opal), it would destroy MV 2 permanents and completely whiff on Nethergoyf. Additionally, even if it hit Nethergoyf, saving EE could have been valuable against Urza's Saga constructs (MV 0) or other threats.

By not playing a land first, Sonnet Coach missed the opportunity to cast both Inquisition of Kozilek AND Thought-Knot Seer in the same turn. With Ifnir Deadlands played first, they'd have 5 mana sources (2 Swamps + Urborg + Urza's Saga + Ifnir Deadlands), enough for Inquisition (1 mana) then TKS (4 mana), stripping two cards from the opponent's hand instead of one.

Failed to activate the existing Emry's tap ability before the second Emry resolves. With the legend rule, one Emry will be sacrificed. By tapping the old Emry now (targeting Mishra's Bauble or Mox Opal in graveyard), they could get value from both the old Emry's tap ability AND the new Emry's ETB mill trigger.

Opponent has Emry on the battlefield with a graveyard full of powerful artifacts (Engineered Explosives, Pithing Needle, Mox Opal, Mishra's Bauble, two Urza's Sagas). Emry's tap ability to recur these artifacts is the opponent's primary engine. Nihil Spellbomb would exile the entire graveyard, stranding Emry with no targets and removing the threat of recurring Engineered Explosives or other powerful artifacts. Pithing Needle naming Emry would also permanently shut down the engine. Shadowspear provides incremental combat advantage but doesn't address the main strategic threat.

The player chose to activate Shadowspear's {1} ability (removing hexproof/indestructible from opponent's permanents) instead of casting a hand disruption spell or equipping Shadowspear. The opponent has no hexproof or indestructible permanents, so this ability accomplishes literally nothing - it wastes 1 mana for zero effect. The player's reasoning says 'equip Shadowspear to Nethergoyf' but they activated the wrong ability ({1} activated ability instead of the {2} equip ability). Meanwhile, they could have cast Thoughtseize or Inquisition of Kozilek to strip a card from the opponent's hand (the opponent likely has Kappa Cannoneer, Metallic Rebuke, or other threats), or they could have actually equipped Shadowspear to Nethergoyf for meaningful combat advantage with lifelink and trample.

Sonnet Coach has 3 untapped Swamps (one regular Swamp plus Urborg makes all lands Swamps, but only one Swamp appears untapped based on the board state). Looking more carefully: bf=[Swamp, Nethergoyf, {'name': 'Swamp', 'tapped': True}, {'name': 'Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth', 'tapped': True}, Shadowspear, Swamp]. There's one untapped Swamp and one other untapped Swamp, so 2 untapped black sources. They could cast Thoughtseize or Inquisition of Kozilek for 1 black mana to strip a card from the opponent's hand. The opponent has Emry on board which can recur artifacts, and seeing their hand is critical. They also skipped attacking with Nethergoyf (which has power equal to card types in graveyard - with Sorcery, Land, Enchantment in the graveyard that's 3/4). The opponent has Emry (1/2) as the only blocker. Attacking would deal at least 1 damage after blocks, or force a trade. Additionally, they could have played Ifnir Deadlands or Urborg from hand as a land drop. Passing the entire turn without casting a hand disruption spell, without playing a land, and without attacking is a significant waste of resources.

Gem25F Libby passed their precombat main phase without casting anything despite having the mana and artifacts to cast Kappa Cannoneer. With Mox Opal (metalcraft active with 4 artifacts), Fiery Islet for mana, and the ability to tap artifacts for Improvise (Welding Jar, Claws of Gix, Pithing Needle, Mox Opal), Kappa Cannoneer costs 5U but with Improvise tapping 4 artifacts only needs U + 1 more mana. Fiery Islet produces U, Mox Opal produces another mana = 2 mana + 4 improvised artifacts = 6 total, exactly enough to cast Kappa Cannoneer. Kappa Cannoneer would enter as a 5/5 (gets a counter on ETB), can't be blocked the turn it enters, has ward 4, and would represent a massive threat against an opponent at 17 life with only a tapped Nethergoyf as a creature. Alternatively, casting Weapons Manufacturing first (1R via Fiery Islet + Mox Opal) would set up powerful synergies with artifacts entering. Passing with a full hand and available mana is a significant missed opportunity.

Playing Prismatic Vista instead of Ifnir Deadlands means Sonnet Coach cannot cast Thought-Knot Seer this turn. Ifnir Deadlands naturally produces {C}, and with Urborg already in play, it also taps for {B}. Playing Ifnir Deadlands would give exactly {3}{B} + {1}{C} = enough to cast Thought-Knot Seer (cost {3}{C}), providing both hand disruption AND a 4/4 body. Instead, they're limited to just Thoughtseize or Inquisition this turn.

The player's reasoning says they want to fetch Eldrazi Temple, but Prismatic Vista can only search for a basic land card. Eldrazi Temple is not a basic land. They will end up fetching a basic Swamp (which they already have 3 of on the battlefield). More importantly, the sequencing is suboptimal - they should cast Thoughtseize or Inquisition of Kozilek first before cracking Vista, since they want to see the opponent's hand to inform their decisions. Additionally, they have Thought-Knot Seer in hand which requires colorless mana ({3}{C}), and fetching a basic Swamp doesn't help cast it since Urborg makes all lands Swamps (producing black). They should have played Ifnir Deadlands from hand instead, which can tap for colorless mana naturally (or black via Urborg) and has utility as removal. Then they could cast a discard spell and still have Prismatic Vista available if needed later.

Nethergoyf is a 3/4 attacking into only Emry (1/2) as a potential blocker. The opponent at 12 life has no profitable block and no combat tricks available. There's no reason to skip attacking - it's 3 free damage with no downside, and attacking doesn't prevent post-combat Thought-Knot Seer.

Exiled Kappa Cannoneer instead of Metallic Rebuke. With both Inquisition of Kozilek and Thoughtseize in hand, exiling the counterspell would have allowed Sonnet Coach to freely resolve discard spells to strip the remaining Kappa Cannoneers. By taking a Cannoneer, the opponent retains Metallic Rebuke to potentially counter the discard spells, making it harder to deal with the second Cannoneer.

Gem25F Libby passed their main phase without casting anything despite the opponent being completely tapped out. They could cast Claws of Gix (0 mana) first to get an additional artifact, then cast Kappa Cannoneer using Improvise (tap Mox Opal for {U}, Fiery Islet for 1 mana at 1 life, and tap 4 artifacts for Improvise). Kappa Cannoneer would enter as a 6/6 (two ETB triggers from Claws and itself), be unblockable that turn, and represent a massive clock. Deploying it while the opponent is tapped out avoids any interaction.

Chose to target Mox Opal with Emry's ability, but there's already a Mox Opal on the battlefield. Due to the legend rule, casting a second would just replace the existing one with no net benefit. Mishra's Bauble would be free to cast, draws a card next upkeep, and adds an extra artifact to the board (helping cast Kappa Cannoneer via improvise). Engineered Explosives could also answer Shadowspear or other threats.

Passed the turn with unused mana and Weapons Manufacturing in hand, which could have been cast for {1}{R} using Mox Opal and Fiery Islet. Weapons Manufacturing is a key engine piece that creates Munitions tokens (dealing 2 damage) whenever nontoken artifacts enter, synergizing powerfully with Emry's artifact recursion and the multiple cheap artifacts in hand/graveyard.

Played a second Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth when one was already on the battlefield. The legend rule forces one to be sacrificed, so this wastes the land drop for the turn and loses a card for no benefit. They needed additional mana sources to cast Thought-Knot Seer or Kozilek's Command.

With the opponent at 5 life, taking Metallic Rebuke might be more impactful than Kappa Cannoneer. Rebuke could counter Kozilek's Command or other key spells needed to close the game. At 5 life, the opponent needs to survive more than deploy 6-mana threats, and ensuring your own spells resolve is critical for closing. Taking one Cannoneer still leaves one in hand.

Both of the opponent's creatures (Nethergoyf and Thought-Knot Seer) are tapped, meaning Emry could attack for 1 unblocked damage with zero risk of being blocked. The tradeoff is losing access to Emry's tap ability this turn to recast an artifact from the graveyard.

Emry's tap ability costs no mana and doesn't compromise the ability to cast Metallic Rebuke. Tapping Emry to target Mishra's Bauble in the graveyard would allow casting it for free, adding an artifact to the battlefield (improving improvise count) and providing card advantage when sacrificed. This is essentially free value that was passed up.
